title: The Peace of God
hookLine: church councils try to protect peasants, pilgrims and clergy from knights' violence

lines: PUT YOUR HAND ON THE SAINTS AND SWEAR.
cards: The saints have been carried out of their churches.

Their relics, in boxes of wood and silver, sit in an open field, and a crowd has walked in from the villages to stand around them: farmers, monks, mothers with children on their hips. Bishops are there too.
So are knights, the men with the horses and the swords, whom nobody, in this time and place, can easily stop. The bishops ask them to put their hands on the relics and swear. Swear to what?
To pax Dei, the Peace of God.

teach.b: In parts of France, there was often no king strong enough to keep order. Local lords and their armed men settled quarrels by raiding, and the ones who suffered were the ones without weapons: peasants, travelers, clergy.
So Church councils named the people who were off limits.

teach.h: THE PEACE: HANDS OFF THE DEFENSELESS.
teach.b: The canons of one such council, at Charroux, are blunt.
Anyone who breaks into a church and robs it, anyone who steals a poor farmer's animals, anyone who strikes a cleric who carries no weapons, is cut off from the Church until he makes amends.
Later councils widened the circle of the protected. A second idea grew beside the first. If the fighting couldn't be ended, maybe it could be paused.
The Truce of God named days of the week and holy seasons, like Advent and Lent, when no one was to fight at all.
The rules differed from council to council, but the shape held: some time belongs to God, and no sword may cross it. The bishops had no army.
What they had was the faith of the crowd, the saints, and Jesus's words, which in the Douay-Rheims read: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."
The Peace and the Truce didn't end the violence, and oaths were broken. But they drew a line around the weak, and said out loud that even a knight answers for whom he hurts.

how: Catholics remember the Peace and Truce of God as an early attempt by the Church to limit violence; today the Church keeps a World Day of Peace each New Year's Day, and parishes pray for peace in the prayers of the faithful.

o: a treaty that ended a war between two kings
a blessing given to knights before a battle
a church oath that shielded the defenseless

games.q: the Peace of God — tap the pairs.
p: days and seasons with no fighting

s: the Peace of God was decreed by a strong king
it came from church councils, where there was often no king strong enough to keep order.
the Truce of God set aside holy seasons like Advent and Lent with no fighting
it named days of the week and holy seasons when no one was to fight.
the Peace and the Truce ended knightly violence
they drew a line around the weak, but oaths were broken and the fighting went on.

games.q: armed men raid the farms, no king can stop them, and the church has no army. what can it do?
o: raise an army of your own.
gather the people and have the knights swear peace on the saints' relics.
stay out of it; it isn't church business.
games.why: councils brought relics and crowds into the fields and asked knights to swear to leave the defenseless alone, cutting off those who broke it.

practice: Let one person come to mind who has less power than the people around them: a new coworker, a child, the one in the group chat everybody talks over.
Hold them without fixing anything, and ask where you could stand between them and some small harm. If you pray, hold them before God with the line, blessed are the peacemakers.

wordCard.voice: Pax Dei. Church councils naming the defenseless, peasants, clergy, travelers, and calling armed men to swear to leave them be. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the peace of God. its partner was the treuga Dei, the truce of God.

carryVoice: Your line: truce of god. Even a pause in the fighting was a kind of peace. Until tomorrow.
